title: Apollo 11: The Eagle Has Landed
crew: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin (Michael Collins in orbit aboard Columbia)
story: 20 July 1969. Eagle is descending toward the Sea of Tranquility when the guidance computer flashes program alarms 1202 and 1201. Mission Control decides it's safe to continue.
Close to the surface, Neil Armstrong sees that the computer is steering them into a boulder field around a crater. He takes semi-manual control and flies on, looking for a clear spot.
In Houston, Charlie Duke calls out fuel: "60 seconds"… "30 seconds". That's the time left before they must land or abort.
goal: Fly past the boulder field and touch down gently before you run out of fuel.
history: Eagle touched down at 20:17:40 UTC on 20 July 1969, a few hundred metres beyond West crater. Post-flight analysis estimated roughly 45 seconds of fuel remained before the abort deadline, more than the "30 seconds" called at the time, because propellant sloshing had fooled the low-level sensor.
facts: The descent engine was the first throttleable rocket engine flown in space.
Lunar gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's, so hovering burns far less fuel than it would on Earth.

sources.title: Descent propulsion system (thrust, throttle range, Isp)
NASA: 50 Years Ago, One Small Step

approximate: Lander mass and fuel at the start of this final approach are estimates for gameplay; the engine figures are the real DPS values.

title: Apollo 13: Get Them Home
crew: Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert, Fred Haise
story: 14 April 1970, 55 h 54 min into the flight. An oxygen tank in the Service Module explodes. The Moon landing is off; now the only goal is getting three astronauts home alive.

The ship is on a "hybrid" trajectory that skims about 110 km above the Moon and would then miss Earth completely. The crew must burn the Lunar Module's descent engine to get back onto a free-return path, one where the Moon's gravity swings them home.
They must hit Earth's atmosphere at just the right angle. Too steep and they burn up; too shallow and they skip off into space.
goal: Burn the LM descent engine to reach Earth's entry corridor: −7.4° to −5.3° at 121.9 km altitude.
history: At 61 h 29 min the crew burned the LM descent engine for about 35 s (≈ 11.6 m/s) to restore a free return. After swinging around the Moon they made the "PC+2" burn (≈ 262 m/s) to speed the trip home. Odyssey splashed down in the Pacific on 17 April 1970.
facts: The burn was done with the Lunar Module steering the whole docked stack, something it was never designed for.
Apollo 13 holds the record for the farthest humans have travelled from Earth.

sources.title: Apollo 13 entry and trajectory notes (NASA NTRS)

approximate: Stack mass, remaining DPS propellant and the throttle (40%) are approximations. Because this game is 2D, the corrective burn needed differs from the real 11.6 m/s.

freeReturn.title: Back to free return
freeReturn.hint: Make a small burn so the predicted path enters Earth’s atmosphere between −7.4° and −5.3°. Watch the entry gauge.

pc2.title: PC+2 burn (bonus)
pc2.hint: After passing the Moon, make a 262 m/s burn that brings the crew home sooner, still inside the corridor.

title: Voyager 2: The Grand Tour
story: In the late 1970s the outer planets lined up in a way that happens only once every 175 years. Voyager 2 can use Jupiter's gravity as a slingshot to reach Saturn, and later Uranus and Neptune.
It's March 1979. Voyager 2 is closing in on Jupiter, but its aim is slightly off. A small trajectory correction now decides whether Jupiter flings it to Saturn or off into empty space.
goal: Make a correction burn so that Jupiter's gravity assist sends Voyager 2 within 1,000,000 km of Saturn.
history: Voyager 2 passed Jupiter on 9 July 1979 (about 570,000 km above the clouds) and Saturn on 26 August 1981. It went on to become the only spacecraft to visit Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989).
facts: A gravity assist steals a tiny bit of a planet's orbital energy. Jupiter slowed down by an immeasurably small amount.
Voyager 2 is now in interstellar space, more than 20 billion km from Earth.
approximate: Spacecraft mass and thruster figures are approximate. The flyby distances and dates come from a trajectory designed to match the real ones in this 2D model.

aim.title: Correct course
aim.hint: A tiny burn now shifts where you pass Jupiter, and that changes everything after. Get the predicted Saturn approach under 1,000,000 km.

saturn.title: Reach Saturn
saturn.hint: Fly through the Jupiter gravity assist all the way to Saturn.

title: Mangalyaan: Mars on the First Try
story: India's first interplanetary mission had a tight budget and a small rocket. The PSLV couldn't throw the spacecraft straight to Mars, so ISRO raised its orbit around Earth six times before the final push.
Launch windows to Mars open only once every 26 months. Pick the departure date and travel time that the spacecraft's fuel can afford.
Then, ten months later, the 440 N main engine must fire for about 23 minutes at Mars, and it hasn't run for 300 days. Too little and Mangalyaan sails past Mars forever.
goal: Choose a launch window, aim for Mars, and fire the engine to enter Mars orbit (periapsis 300–800 km).
history: Launched on 5 November 2013 on PSLV-C25, Mangalyaan left Earth on 1 December 2013 and fired its engine for 1,388.67 s on 24 September 2014. It entered a 421.7 × 76,993.6 km Mars orbit, making India the first nation to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt.
facts: The Mars Orbiter Mission was famously cheaper than the film Gravity.
MOM's orbit took 72 hours 51 minutes, which is why its photos could capture the whole disc of Mars.
approximate: Mass after the Earth-orbit raising burns (1,012 kg) is an estimate. The LAM specific impulse (315 s) is approximate.

tcm.title: Trajectory correction
tcm.hint: Months before arrival, a small burn moves your closest approach to Mars to 300–800 km altitude.

moi.title: Mars orbit insertion
moi.hint: At closest approach, burn retrograde relative to Mars for about 20+ minutes. Too short and you fly past Mars forever.

title: Perseverance: Seven Minutes of Terror
story: 18 February 2021. Perseverance hits the top of Mars's atmosphere at about 19,500 km/h. Radio signals take over 11 minutes to reach Earth, so everything happens on its own.
The capsule rolls its lift up or down to steer. When it has slowed enough, the supersonic parachute opens, and that only works within a narrow window.
Finally the descent stage fires its rockets and lowers the rover on cables: the sky crane.
goal: Steer the entry, open the parachute in its safe window, then fly the descent stage to a safe spot in Jezero Crater.
history: The parachute opened about 240 s after entry, at about 11 km altitude and 1,512 km/h. Powered descent began at 2.1 km, and the sky crane lowered the rover 6.4 m on cables. Perseverance touched down in Jezero Crater at about 20:55 UTC.
facts: Terrain-Relative Navigation let Perseverance compare camera images with a map and divert to a safer spot. It was a first for Mars.
The 21.5 m parachute had to open at almost twice the speed of sound.

sources.title: NASA JPL Mars 2020 landing press kit

approximate: Entry mass, aerodynamic coefficients, parachute limits and descent-stage mass are approximate public figures. Mars's rotation and cross-range steering are not modelled.

title: Chandrayaan-3: Earth to the Moon
story: 14 July 2023: LVM3 launches Chandrayaan-3 from Sriharikota into an Earth orbit of about 170 × 36,500 km.
There isn't enough rocket to fly straight to the Moon, so the Propulsion Module's 440 N engine raises the orbit step by step, firing each time it swings past perigee.
Then comes trans-lunar injection, timed so the Moon is waiting when the craft arrives, and a braking burn to be captured into lunar orbit.
goal: Raise your orbit, fly to the Moon and fire a braking burn to enter lunar orbit (periapsis 100–1,000 km, apoapsis below 20,000 km).
history: After five Earth-bound burns, trans-lunar injection came on 1 August 2023 (IST). Lunar orbit insertion on 5 August placed Chandrayaan-3 in a 164 × 18,074 km orbit, later circularised to 153 × 163 km.
facts: Chandrayaan-3 took about 40 days to reach the Moon. Apollo took about 3, but needed a giant Saturn V rocket.
The Propulsion Module later returned to Earth orbit: a bonus test of ISRO's navigation skills.
approximate: The Propulsion Module engine's specific impulse is approximate. The perigee direction is chosen so the real Moon is reachable on similar dates.

raise.title: Raise your orbit
raise.hint: Burn prograde at perigee (closest to Earth). Each burn lifts the far side of the orbit. Get the apogee above 100,000 km.

tli.title: Trans-lunar injection
tli.hint: From perigee, burn prograde again so the orbit stretches out to where the Moon WILL be when you arrive. Watch the dashed prediction meet the Moon.

loi.title: Lunar orbit insertion
loi.hint: At closest approach to the Moon, burn retrograde (against your motion relative to the Moon) to be captured. Aim for 100–1,000 km periapsis and apoapsis below 20,000 km.

circular.title: Circularise (bonus)
circular.hint: Lower the orbit to under 200 km with braking burns at perilune, like ISRO did.

title: Chandrayaan-3: Vikram at the South Pole
story: 23 August 2023. Vikram is descending near the Moon's south pole, where no spacecraft had ever landed softly.
At about 150 m it pauses and hovers, and its hazard camera searches for flat, boulder-free ground.
Its four 800 N engines must set the lander down gently: its legs can take no more than about 3 m/s.
goal: Hover, pick a safe spot from the hazard map, and land at under 3 m/s.
history: Vikram touched down at 12:33 UTC (18:03 IST) on 23 August 2023 at 69.373°S, 32.319°E. India became the first country to land near the lunar south pole. Pragyan rolled out the next day and confirmed sulphur in the soil.
facts: The landing site is now called Shiv Shakti Point.
Vikram later "hopped": it re-fired its engines, rose about 40 cm and landed again 30–40 cm away.

sources.title: Chandrayaan-3 (lander mass, engines, landing site, time)

approximate: Mass and fuel at 800 m, engine Isp and the minimum throttle are estimates; engine count and thrust are real.

title: Aditya-L1: Parking at L1
story: 1.5 million km from Earth, toward the Sun, there is a point where the Sun's and Earth's pulls balance out: Lagrange point L1. From there, a telescope can watch the Sun without ever being blocked.
But L1 is like balancing a ball on a hill. Leave a spacecraft there and it slowly rolls away.
6 January 2024: Aditya-L1 fires its engine for halo-orbit insertion. After that, small station-keeping burns keep it circling L1.
goal: Keep Aditya-L1 near L1 for one full orbit (178 days), using as little fuel as possible.
history: Aditya-L1 launched on 2 September 2023 on PSLV-C57, cruised for about 110 days and entered its halo orbit on 6 January 2024. It completed its first revolution around L1 in about 178 days, on 2 July 2024.
facts: L1 is about 1% of the way from Earth to the Sun.
NASA's SOHO observatory has watched the Sun from L1 since 1996.
approximate: This is a 2D game, so the real 3D halo orbit is shown as its planar cousin, a Lyapunov orbit with the same 178-day period. The fuel load is approximate.

hold.title: Hold the halo orbit
hold.hint: Stay inside the box around L1 for 178 days. Small burns every few weeks keep you on the reference orbit (dotted).
